Machine-learning methods are often called assumption-free. They make fewer assumptions
about the shape of a relationship than a linear model does, but they still assume the
data were collected in a way that lets the stations stand for the ocean. The section
takes each assumption in turn, on the same simulated survey as the rest of the course.
The first two pages cover what a model assumes about shape and spread, which machine
learning relaxes:

- **linearity and nonlinearity**: a generalised additive model gives each input its own
  smooth curve, fits the stations best, and still gets one curve wrong;
- **distributional assumptions**: simulating surveys from a fitted count model shows
  whether it could have produced the real one.

The next three cover how the data were collected, which it does not relax:

- **independence of observations**: repeat visits to a site are worth fewer stations
  than their number, and resampling whole sites measures how many fewer;
- **spatial and temporal dependence**: neighbouring sites share their water, and
  holding out whole areas of the map measures what a model knows without them;
- **uneven sampling and extrapolation**: each method carries on past the survey in its
  own way, and the distance to the nearest surveyed station shows where that happens.

The last page takes a rare answer:

- **class imbalance**: sensitivity, specificity and precision count misses and false
  alarms apart, and rebalancing the training data turns out to move the threshold.

The section picks up threads from earlier ones. The penalty on bending in
[Linearity and nonlinearity](linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd) works like the ridge penalty
in [Regularisation](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd).
[Distributional assumptions](distributional-assumptions.qmd) tests the negative binomial
model from [Count regression](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd).
[Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) kept each site's visits on one
side of the split; [Independence of observations](independence-of-observations.qmd)
measures what those visits are worth. Cross-validation by site from
[Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) scores every
model here, and [Spatial and temporal dependence](spatial-and-temporal-dependence.qmd)
compares it with spatial blocks, which
[Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd)
develops. [Class imbalance](class-imbalance.qmd) builds on the misses and false alarms of
[Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) and leaves
whole-curve scores to [Classification metrics](../07-validation/classification-metrics.qmd).

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [spatialsample](https://spatialsample.tidymodels.org/), tidymodels. Blocked, clustered and buffered resampling for data with a location, which is the concrete answer to most of this section.
- [Common pitfalls and recommended practices](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html), scikit-learn. Independence is assumed silently in almost every default, and this page says where.
